title:
A shared brain.
A practical starting point.
example: Explore how reviewed AI assistance could connect work across Big Tiny, from finance to the guest experience.
inputs: Public company context and a working local proof of concept; no internal operating baseline.
approval: Discussion proposals only. Functional leaders choose which problems deserve a pilot.
staff: Less time assembling context; more time acting on it.
customer: Clearer commitments and more dependable follow-through — hypotheses to test.
metric: Judge useful outcomes, not the number of agents.
narration: This presentation explores how reviewed AI assistance could support Big Tiny across the business, from finance and sales to delivery and guest service. It is an opportunity discussion, not an approved roadmap. The aim is to reduce administrative effort and improve follow through. We should test those benefits before making commitments.

title:
Working mechanism today.
Broader tools are proposals.
example: CURRENT: paste a note → extract facts → propose create, update or clarify → review → human approval → local task memory.
inputs: One pasted note and saved tasks. Three prompts use the same on-prem model.
approval: Notes and agent outputs persist before approval. Only task mutations wait for approval.
staff: See a proposal and its evidence before changing saved work.
customer: No customer-facing actions are currently performed.
metric: Real fictional-example tests passed; staff productivity is not yet measured.
narration: The working proof of concept accepts a note, proposes task changes or questions, reviews the result, and waits for a person to approve. It remembers local tasks. Notes and agent outputs are saved before approval; task changes are not. Everything else in this presentation, including source connections and departmental tools, is a proposed extension.

title:
Three relationships.
Different definitions of value.
example:
GUESTS: accurate information and a prepared stay.
OWNERS: clear, supported updates.
LANDOWNER PARTNERS: transparent requirements and handoffs.
inputs: Big Tiny's public modular hospitality, property-management and ownership context.
approval: Actual service promises and contractual commitments remain with authorised people.
staff: Make the intended beneficiary explicit for every proposed tool.
customer: Some benefits are direct; finance, HR and IT benefits are often indirect.
metric: Check relevant service outcomes alongside internal effort.
narration: Customer value is not a single category. Guests need accurate information and a prepared stay. Tiny house owners need clear updates supported by records. Landowner partners need transparent requirements and reliable handoffs. Some tools could help directly. Others, such as finance or staff knowledge support, would benefit customers indirectly through better internal work.

title:
Start with evidence.
Keep decisions with people.
example: Authorised sources → bounded planning and lookup → draft → review → human decision → restricted action, only if approved.
inputs: Optional read-only documents and records, with source identity, permissions and freshness.
approval: No automatic cloud fallback. No autonomous payments, refunds, hiring or professional sign-off.
staff: Cited drafts and visible gaps rather than unsupported certainty.
customer: Commitments remain accountable and checked.
metric: Source coverage, correction burden and permission failures.
narration: A future shared service would need authentication, permissions and reliable records. Begin with read only information and cited drafts. Add planning, lookup or review roles only when they help the chosen workflow. Human approval must precede external writes or sends. There is no automatic cloud fallback, and the model cannot replace professional sign off.

title:
Find billing exceptions
before they become a chase.
example: “This supplier invoice does not match the purchase order. Show the discrepancy and draft the follow-up.”
inputs: Authorised invoices, purchase orders, receipts and account balances.
approval: Finance verifies calculations and postings; people approve payments and collection sends.
staff: Less manual matching and document assembly.
customer: Indirect: clearer billing and fewer avoidable queries.
metric: Exception precision and total review time.
narration: For accounts payable and receivable, consider an exception assistant. It could compare an invoice with the order and receipt, then draft a specific follow up. Deterministic calculations and verified records should establish the amounts. Finance checks the result and retains control over postings, payments and customer communications. Measure exception accuracy and review time.

title:
Explain a variance
with numbers that reconcile.
example: “Why did maintenance spending differ from budget? Separate supported facts from possible explanations.”
inputs: Approved budgets, verified actuals, reporting definitions and explanatory records.
approval: Finance validates reconciled numbers; management approves budgets and allocation decisions.
staff: Less briefing assembly, more attention to meaningful exceptions.
customer: Indirect: better-informed allocation of service resources.
metric: Reconciliation errors, unsupported explanations and preparation time.
narration: Financial planning could use a cited variance brief rather than a fresh narrative assembled each month. The tool would link verified actuals and budgets to supporting records, keeping untested explanations separate. Calculations should reconcile outside the language model. Finance validates the brief, and management decides what to change. No financial return is promised.

title:
Turn an enquiry into
a clearer scope discussion.
example: “Summarise this buyer's requirements and highlight questions before we prepare a proposal.”
inputs: Consented enquiry, approved specifications, current prices and proposal templates.
approval: Sales approves scope, prices, terms and every external proposal.
staff: Less repeated proposal assembly and fewer missing requirements.
customer: A clearer understanding of what is included and still unresolved.
metric: Missing requirements, proposal rework and preparation time.
narration: A sales assistant could turn an enquiry into a requirements summary and a list of unanswered questions. It would use approved specifications and current prices, not invent capabilities or terms. Sales would approve the proposal before it reaches a buyer. The test is whether preparation becomes easier while customers receive a clearer, more accurate scope.

title:
Create faster first drafts.
Keep claims grounded.
example: “Draft a campaign brief for this property using only approved features and consented images.”
inputs: Brand guidance, verified property facts, approved claims and licensed or consented assets.
approval: Marketing checks claims, rights and publication. No invented accessibility or pet-policy promises.
staff: Less time starting from a blank page.
customer: More accurate expectations before enquiry or booking.
metric: Factual corrections and review-to-publication effort.
narration: Marketing could gain a useful first draft without giving the model permission to publish. A brief would draw from approved features, brand guidance and permitted assets. A person would check factual claims and rights. Accessibility, pet policies and environmental statements need explicit evidence. Measure correction burden as well as the time saved on drafting.

title:
Surface booking exceptions.
Suggest; do not change live rates.
example: “Show booking inconsistencies and prepare questions for the next demand review.”
inputs: Fresh availability, booking records, approved rates, policies and reporting definitions.
approval: Authorised staff approve booking, inventory and live rate changes.
staff: Less cross-checking across reservation information.
customer: Fewer contradictory availability or price statements.
metric: Exception accuracy, data freshness and handling time.
narration: Reservations and revenue teams could review booking exceptions and demand summaries. The distinction matters: analysis and suggestions do not change live rates or bookings. Availability and price statements require fresh records. Authorised staff decide and execute any change. Evaluate the accuracy of flagged exceptions and the effort required to resolve them, not a promised revenue uplift.

title:
Answer the actual question
with the current policy.
example: “Draft a response to this guest's arrival question and flag any facts we cannot confirm.”
inputs: Permitted guest enquiry, relevant booking, fresh property information and current policies.
approval: Staff approve every send, refund, relocation or service remedy.
staff: Less repetitive writing and easier escalation summaries.
customer: Clearer, more consistent answers without invented promises.
metric: Response preparation time and factual correction rate.
narration: A guest service assistant could draft an answer with the applicable policy and identify information that still needs checking. It should not guess availability, prices or property features. Staff approve all messages and decide refunds or other remedies. The intended customer benefit is clearer communication, tested through factual accuracy and the effort needed to review each draft.

title:
Make the next shift
a continuation, not a reset.
example: “Prepare today's handover: unresolved jobs, changed plans, owners and questions.”
inputs: Authorised staff updates, current task register and reliable property identifiers.
approval: Operations checks assignments and task closures. Existing register remains authoritative during a pilot.
staff: Less status chasing and handover rewriting.
customer: Better follow-through on issues affecting a stay.
metric: Missed actions, matching accuracy and net review time.
narration: Property operations is close to the existing proof of concept. A proposed next step is a draft daily handover that connects updates with unresolved jobs. Staff would check the property, owner and next action before accepting it. The current operational register should remain authoritative during evaluation. Measure missed actions and total staff effort, including review.

title:
Prioritise turnover work.
Show readiness evidence gaps.
example: “Which upcoming turnovers have an incomplete checklist or a reported supply shortage?”
inputs: Fresh arrival and departure information, cleaning checklists and approved supply records.
approval: A supervisor confirms physical readiness; a model cannot inspect a room.
staff: Clearer priorities and earlier escalation of missing information.
customer: A better-prepared arrival, if operational checks confirm it.
metric: Missed checklist items and time from blocker report to escalation.
narration: Housekeeping could use a turnover exception list that highlights incomplete checks or supply shortages before an arrival. This requires fresh schedules and reliable cleaning records. The output is a prompt to verify, not an all clear. A supervisor still confirms physical readiness. Measure missing checklist items and how early genuine blockers are escalated.

title:
Connect repeat reports
without guessing a diagnosis.
example: “Is this a follow-up to the same water-system issue? Show the supporting record and next question.”
inputs: Work orders, equipment identifiers, staff reports and service history.
approval: Qualified staff approve diagnosis, dispatch and repair completion.
staff: Less duplicate reporting and easier follow-up preparation.
customer: Fewer unresolved faults and clearer repair communication.
metric: Correct task matches, duplicate reports and unsupported closures.
narration: Maintenance support could connect follow ups to the same equipment issue and assemble its service history. Pattern summaries may suggest an investigation, but they do not establish a root cause. Qualified staff retain diagnosis, dispatch and completion decisions. Evaluate matching accuracy and duplicate reporting, with particular attention to any proposed closure that lacks confirmation.

title:
Compare the same scope.
Make exclusions visible.
example: “Compare these repair quotes and identify missing parts, exclusions and delivery assumptions.”
inputs: Authorised quotes, required specifications, stock records and purchasing rules.
approval: Buyers verify calculations and suppliers; people approve orders and spending.
staff: Less document comparison and fewer overlooked exclusions.
customer: Indirect: fewer missing materials that delay service.
metric: Omitted exclusions and comparison review time.
narration: Procurement could compare quotations against the same required scope, exposing exclusions instead of ranking prices alone. Inventory exceptions could highlight missing materials. Amounts and comparisons need deterministic checks against verified records. Buyers select suppliers and approve orders. Measure whether important exclusions are retained and whether the full comparison takes less staff time.

title:
Trace a requirement
through the revision trail.
example: “Which requirements or downstream documents need review after this drawing revision?”
inputs: Controlled drawings, approved specifications, revision history and applicable requirements.
approval: Qualified professionals retain all engineering, safety and design sign-off.
staff: Easier first-pass cross-checking and change summaries.
customer: Better-documented requirement coverage, not an AI safety certification.
metric: Missed requirements, incorrect revision references and rework.
narration: Engineering and design could use requirement tracing and revision summaries to prepare a review. The system would need controlled drawings and specifications, not uncontrolled copies. It might identify a downstream document needing attention, but qualified professionals retain every engineering and safety sign off. The value test is fewer missed requirements and less review rework.

title:
Assemble the quality story
from the inspection evidence.
example: “Prepare this unit's defect and inspection pack; show missing evidence before release review.”
inputs: Controlled bills of materials, inspection records, unit identifiers and defect reports.
approval: The quality lead approves release, rejection and corrective action.
staff: Less report consolidation across production records.
customer: More traceable quality checks before delivery.
metric: Evidence completeness and report preparation time.
narration: Manufacturing and quality teams could receive an inspection evidence pack organised around a unit and its defects. Missing records should remain explicit rather than becoming a guessed pass. The quality lead decides release or rejection and any corrective action. Measure traceability completeness and report preparation effort, while preserving the existing quality process.

title:
Expose the dependency
before the delivery date.
example: “List unconfirmed site-access, delivery and installation prerequisites for this handover.”
inputs: Authorised shipment status, site checklist, installation plan and responsible contacts.
approval: Responsible leads approve dispatch, installation decisions and site acceptance.
staff: Earlier visibility of incomplete handoffs.
customer: Clearer delivery expectations and fewer surprise prerequisites.
metric: Missing prerequisites discovered late and schedule corrections.
narration: Logistics and installation support could surface a dependency that is easy to lose between teams, such as unconfirmed site access. It would assemble an evidence based handover rather than make delivery promises. Responsible leads approve dispatch and site acceptance. Track prerequisites discovered too late and the effort spent reconciling schedule changes.

title:
Ask the missing site question
before making a commitment.
example: “Prepare an initial site brief and identify evidence still needed for specialist assessment.”
inputs: Consented site information, approved screening criteria and applicable specialist requirements.
approval: Specialists determine feasibility; authorised people approve partner commitments.
staff: Less repeated questionnaire assembly and earlier information gaps.
customer: Landowner partners receive clearer requirements and next steps.
metric: Missing evidence and initial screening preparation time.
narration: For landowner partnerships and expansion, a tool could organise an initial site brief and its unanswered questions. Public information or a completed form cannot prove feasibility. Specialists must assess the site, and authorised people approve commitments. The potential partner benefit is a clearer process. Measure missing evidence and the effort required to prepare the first review.

title:
Prepare an owner update
that can be traced to records.
example: “Draft an update on this owner's unit using approved statements and relevant maintenance facts.”
inputs: Authorised ownership records, applicable agreements, approved statements and service history.
approval: Owner-relations and finance staff verify statements and approve the send.
staff: Less cross-team information assembly.
customer: Owners receive clearer, supported communication without new return promises.
metric: Statement corrections and enquiry handling effort.
narration: Owner relations could assemble an update from authorised records and approved statements. This is different from guest communication and must respect the owner's specific agreement. Finance and owner relations check the facts before sending. The system must not create financial return promises. Evaluate statement corrections and the time needed to answer an owner's enquiry.

title:
Help people find the procedure
and leave a clearer handover.
example: “Draft a sourced onboarding guide, translate an approved instruction, or extract meeting follow-ups.”
inputs: Approved policies, role guides, permitted training records and consented meeting notes.
approval: HR approves policy guidance; staff check translations and actions. No autonomous employment decisions.
staff: Less repeated explanation and easier cross-border coordination.
customer: Indirect: better-informed teams and more consistent service.
metric: Answer accuracy, translation corrections and search or follow-up time.
narration: Staff support can include sourced onboarding, meeting follow ups and cross border language assistance. Translation still needs a competent reviewer, particularly for safety or policy instructions. Use approved guides and permitted notes, with no autonomous hiring or employment decisions. The hypothesis is less repeated explanation and clearer coordination, measured through accuracy and staff effort.

title:
Find the right answer
within the right permissions.
example: “Show the approved procedure I am allowed to access, with its owner and revision.”
inputs: Approved knowledge, source access rules, document revisions and sanitised incident records.
approval: IT approves access and operational changes. The model does not grant permissions.
staff: Less searching through outdated or irrelevant documents.
customer: Indirect: more dependable support and information handling.
metric: Citation accuracy, search effort and unauthorised disclosures.
narration: Knowledge support should return the approved procedure a person is allowed to see, with its source and revision. Access control must be enforced by the system, not delegated to a prompt. IT retains operational change decisions. Evaluate cited answer accuracy and search effort, and treat any unauthorised disclosure as a serious failure requiring investigation.

title:
Prepare the comparison.
Keep interpretation accountable.
example: “Compare this draft with our approved template and list obligations requiring counsel's review.”
inputs: Authorised contracts, relevant jurisdiction and counsel-approved templates.
approval: Counsel approves legal advice; authorised signatories approve terms and commitments.
staff: Less first-pass extraction and document comparison.
customer: Clearer, checked commitments; no automated legal assurance.
metric: Missed obligations and reviewer corrections.
narration: Legal and compliance assistance could prepare clause comparisons and obligation checklists for a professional reviewer. Relevant jurisdiction and approved templates are essential. It does not provide final legal advice or establish compliance. Counsel and authorised signatories retain those decisions. Measure missed obligations and corrections rather than treating a fluent summary as a reliable conclusion.

title:
Build the evidence
before making the claim.
example: “Which environmental statements have supporting measurements, and where is evidence missing?”
inputs: Verified measurements, stated methods, supplier evidence and reporting boundaries.
approval: Responsible specialists validate methods and approve environmental claims.
staff: Less manual evidence collection and clearer reporting gaps.
customer: More substantiated environmental information.
metric: Evidence coverage and unsupported claims found in review.
narration: Sustainability support should begin with an evidence register. It could connect a proposed statement to measurements and methods, or flag the absence of support. Responsible specialists approve the methodology and the claim. The intended customer benefit is better substantiated information, not an assumed environmental result. Measure evidence coverage and unsupported claims caught during review.

title:
Compare options
without hiding assumptions.
example: “Prepare an options memo: evidence, constraints, uncertainties and a small test for each direction.”
inputs: Approved internal reports, cited external research, decision criteria and constraints.
approval: Leaders choose strategy, resources and experiments. Research does not authorise action.
staff: Less briefing assembly and a clearer basis for discussion.
customer: Indirect: better-informed service and product priorities.
metric: Source coverage, corrected assumptions and decision preparation effort.
narration: Leadership could use a structured options memo that distinguishes evidence, assumptions and unresolved questions. Internal reports and external research need citations and an agreed scope. The useful output is a clearer decision, not a recommendation that executes itself. Leaders choose resources and experiments. Measure preparation effort and source quality, without claiming an unmeasured return on investment.

title:
A guest fault
before arrival.
example: Housekeeping reports a water fault → operations connects the arrival → maintenance checks → guest service prepares communication → finance checks later invoice exceptions.
inputs: Fictional scenario. Future integrations need fresh arrival, task, equipment and policy records.
approval: People confirm diagnosis and physical readiness, then decide messages, relocation or refunds.
staff: One evidence trail instead of repeated status reconstruction.
customer: Earlier, clearer communication and a prepared stay — to be measured.
metric: Blockers surfaced earlier, handoff completeness and total checking effort.
narration: Imagine a fictional water fault shortly before arrival. A reviewed workflow could connect the cleaner's report, the maintenance record and a fresh arrival schedule, then prepare the handover and guest briefing. People still confirm the repair and physical readiness, and approve any message, relocation or refund. A closed task alone does not prove a property is safe or ready.

title:
A new property launch.
One dependency trail.
example: Partner enquiry → site review → design → procurement → production → delivery → operational handover → approved launch communication.
inputs: Fictional scenario. Controlled site, drawing, quality, delivery and readiness records would be required.
approval: Each specialist validates their record; management approves commitments and launch timing.
staff: Expose missing prerequisites and revision mismatches across teams.
customer: Partners, owners and guests receive more consistent expectations.
metric: Late prerequisite discoveries, revision mismatches and reconciliation time.
narration: For a fictional new property launch, an evidence checklist could expose a missing site answer or a drawing revision before it disrupts procurement or handover. Each team validates its own record. Specialists retain professional sign off, and management approves launch timing. Marketing and reservations use approved facts only. The test is whether handoff gaps become visible earlier.

title:
Choose one useful workflow.
Earn the next integration.
example: START: handover and maintenance follow-up, closest to today’s POC → NEXT: sourced SOP lookup and quote comparison when records are ready → INTEGRATE after evidence.
inputs: Representative authorised examples, a named owner, current baseline and independent review labels.
approval: Read-only and document assistance first. Transactional connections are a later decision.
staff: Start where repetition is high and checking is manageable.
customer: Track a relevant service outcome, not only internal output volume.
metric: Net staff time, accuracy, citations, missed actions and correction burden.
narration: Do not build twenty tools at once. Start with handover and maintenance follow up, closest to today’s proof of concept. Consider sourced procedure lookup and quote comparison next, when the records are ready. Choose an accountable owner, authorised examples and a reviewer. Run in shadow mode and measure total effort, including checking. Add transactional integrations only if evidence and controls justify them.

title:
Agree the problem.
Name the owner. Test the value.
example: Select one workflow, one accountable owner, authorised sample data, a baseline and a pilot review date. Keep the current system authoritative.
inputs: Confirmed data access, a baseline, success measures and critical-error stop rules.
approval: This is a discovery decision, not a company-wide implementation commitment.
staff: Extend only the workflows that prove useful to the people doing the work.
customer: Keep guest, owner and partner outcomes visible in each decision.
metric: Proceed, revise or stop based on measured evidence.
narration: The management decision is to select one workflow worth testing, name its owner, and agree authorised sample data, a baseline and a pilot review date. Keep the current system authoritative while evaluating. Compare against the manual process and a simpler alternative. If the evidence supports improvement, extend one workflow at a time. Otherwise revise or stop. Let useful outcomes guide the next step.
